indiaMissions/india-thomas-christians/ti: The St Thomas Christians of Kerala
indiaMissions/india-thomas-christians/su: The St Thomas Christians (Nasranis, Mar Thoma Nasranis) of Kerala trace their church to the apostle Thomas, said to have landed at Muziris in AD 52 and to have been killed near Mylapore around 72. The apostolic founding cannot be proved, but a Syriac-using church with bishops from the Church of the East is securely attested on the Malabar coast by the sixth century at the latest. For more than a thousand years the Nasranis lived as a high-status trading and landholding community woven into Kerala's caste society, “Hindu in culture, Christian in religion and Oriental in worship”, before Portuguese intervention split them into the many Syrian churches of today.
indiaMissions/india-thomas-christians/st:
Kerala tradition holds that the apostle Thomas arrived at Muziris (Kodungallur) in AD 52, converted several Brahmin families and founded seven and a half churches: Kodungallur, Palayur, Kottakkavu (Paravur), Kokkamangalam, Niranam, Nilackal (Chayal), Kollam and the “half church” (Arappally) at Thiruvithamcode. He is said to have crossed to the Coromandel coast and been speared to death near Mylapore around 72. The earliest written account, the Syriac Acts of Thomas (Edessa, early third century), sends Thomas to the court of King Gondophares — a real Indo-Parthian ruler of the north-west, known from coins and the Takht-i-Bahi inscription — which shows that its author knew something genuine about first-century India. Church fathers from Ephrem to Jerome linked Thomas with India, and Eusebius reports that Pantaenus of Alexandria (c. 180) found Christians in “India”, although that word could also mean Arabia or Ethiopia. Busy Roman trade with Muziris, confirmed by the Muziris papyrus and the Pattanam excavations, makes an early mission plausible, but historians such as Stephen Neill and Robert Frykenberg conclude that it can be neither proved nor disproved. Kerala's own oral tradition, preserved in songs such as the Thomma Parvam (Ramban Pattu), was written down only in the early modern period.

Firmer ground comes with the Church of the East. The Alexandrian merchant Cosmas Indicopleustes (c. 550) reported Christians in “Male, where the pepper grows” and a bishop at Kalliana ordained in Persia. Community tradition dates a migration of some 72 Syrian Christian families under the merchant Thomas of Cana (Knai Thomman) to around 345; their descendants, the Knanaya or “Southists”, have kept strict endogamy ever since, distinct from the “Northist” majority. A second arrival of Persian clergy, Mar Sapor and Mar Prodh, at Kollam around 825 is remembered in the founding of churches, and the Tharisappalli copper plates of 849 confirm that a Christian merchant guild and church in Kollam enjoyed royal privileges. Bishops came from Mesopotamia and used the East Syriac liturgy of Addai and Mari; daily leadership lay with an Indian archdeacon (the Jathikku Karthavyan, “head of the community”).

The Nasranis were integrated into Kerala society as a high caste, ranked alongside the Nairs. Rulers granted them privileges such as riding elephants, using palanquins, carrying swords and collecting certain dues; they were prominent in the pepper trade and served as soldiers trained in kalari martial arts. They observed caste purity — avoiding contact with Pulaya and Paraya labourers — and many owned agrestic slaves until Travancore abolished slavery in 1855. Their churches resembled temples, with flagstaffs, lamps and processions; their marriage rites included the tali; and they shared festivals and customs with Hindu neighbours. The Carmelite historian Placid Podipara later summed this up in the formula “Hindu (Indian) in culture, Christian in religion and Oriental in worship”. The community was devout but not, for most of its history, outwardly missionary: it reproduced itself as a caste rather than seeking converts.

The arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498 began a new era. Leaders of the community welcomed the Portuguese as fellow Christians and potential protectors, and in 1504 East Syriac bishops in Kerala wrote to their patriarch that there were some 30,000 Christian families in Malabar. Portuguese clergy soon treated Syriac practice as “Nestorian” heresy. Latinisation culminated in the Synod of Diamper (1599) and provoked the Coonan Cross Oath of 1653, which split the community into the Catholic Pazhayakoor (“old allegiance”) and the independent Puthenkoor (“new allegiance”), which in 1665 adopted the West Syriac (Antiochene) tradition (see the Diamper and Coonan Cross entry).

Further divisions followed. The Malabar Independent Syrian Church at Thozhiyur separated in 1772. Contact with the Church Missionary Society's “Mission of Help” (from 1816) inspired the reformer Abraham Malpan, whose movement became the Mar Thoma Syrian Church (separated by the Royal Court of Travancore ruling of 1889); evangelicals later left it to form the St Thomas Evangelical Church (1961). A group that sought renewed links with the East Syriac patriarch became the Chaldean Syrian Church of Thrissur. The Puthenkoor itself divided between the autocephalous Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church (catholicate 1912) and the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church loyal to the Syriac Orthodox patriarch of Antioch, a dispute over churches and property that went to India's Supreme Court in 1958, 1995 and 2017. In 1930 Mar Ivanios led part of the Orthodox into communion with Rome as the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, while the Catholic Pazhayakoor received Indian bishops in 1896 and became the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church, a major-archiepiscopal church from 1992.

In the twentieth century the Syrian churches turned outward. The Mar Thoma Evangelistic Association (1888), the Syro-Malabar missionary congregations such as the Missionary Society of St Thomas (1968), and thousands of Kerala priests, nuns, nurses and teachers carried Kerala Christianity to north India, the Gulf and the West; in 2017 Rome gave the Syro-Malabar Church jurisdiction throughout India. Yet relations with Dalit converts brought into Syrian churches by nineteenth-century missions were often marked by separate congregations and discrimination, a grievance voiced sharply by Poykayil Yohannan, who left the Mar Thoma church to found the Prathyaksha Raksha Daiva Sabha in 1909. In the 2011 census Kerala had about 6.14 million Christians, 18.4 per cent of the state's population.

indiaMissions/india-thomas-christians/le: The St Thomas Christians give Indian Christianity its claim to be as old as Christianity itself and not a colonial import. Their history also shows the cost of deep inculturation: a church thoroughly Indian in custom absorbed caste along with culture. Their fragmentation into eight or more churches under Portuguese, Syriac Orthodox, Anglican and Roman influences mirrors the wider history of world Christianity in a single Kerala community.
